BPM Justification: Value stream mapping is BPM process modeling under a different name; extending it with environmental metrics is a direct addition to the process model and its associated data, not a generic engineering practice.

Choosing which environmental metrics to track per process, rather than applying one fixed set everywhere, is a process-specific analysis decision even though it stops short of changing the process's structure.
This is the same move as GBPP's Common Process Improvement pattern: folding an environmental dimension into standard process-improvement analysis, which is a core BPM concern by definition.

The taxonomy is applied per process step, giving it a real process-analysis connection, but the seven waste categories themselves (energy, water, materials, transportation, emissions, biodiversity) are generic environmental-impact categories, not BPM constructs.

A structured walk-and-quantify observation of a running process to drive improvement decisions is functionally the same class of technique as process mining or direct process observation in BPM's analysis phase.
Putting environmental KPIs on the same monitoring boards as operational process metrics is a process-monitoring practice, not a generic facilities-management one.

Identical in substance to GBPP.PROC.1 and the PPA automation-style patterns: standard BPM process optimization, just with an explicit environmental criterion added to the usual time/cost/quality ones.
A checklist used specifically during process-review events ties this to BPM's analysis phase, though it's a facilitation aid for that analysis rather than a change to the process itself.

Bringing subject-matter expertise into redesign work early to avoid late-stage rework is generically true of any design effort, not something specific to business processes; it's anchored to the Design phase but doesn't argue anything BPM-particular.

This is chemical/material lifecycle-and-health guidance that only applies to processes with physical material inputs, and the underlying argument (don't just reduce volume, check toxicity/persistence too) is generic environmental-health advice rather than a BPM-specific concern.
